lead: An oscillator makes a periodic RF signal without an input; a VCO lets a voltage tune its frequency. Phase noise measures how much of that signal's power spreads into nearby offsets, in dBc/Hz. A frequency synthesizer locks a VCO to a stable reference using a PLL, so the output has the reference's long-term accuracy and the VCO's fast tuning. These blocks supply the local oscillator for mixers in receivers and transmitters; see 5.7.
prereq: You need: the LO port of a mixer in 5.7 and noise density in 5.2.

blocks.text: An oscillator is an amplifier that feeds part of its output back to its input with the right phase. The loop starts from thermal noise. At one frequency the phase shift around the loop is 0° (or a whole number of 360° turns) and the loop gain magnitude is at least one. The signal grows; then the amplifier saturates and the gain falls to exactly one. This is the Barkhausen condition.

blocks.where: A is the amplifier voltage gain; β is the feedback fraction; Aβ is the loop gain.

blocks.text: The same idea appears as a negative-resistance one-port. An LC tank has loss; an active device supplies a negative resistance that cancels it. The tank sets frequency and Q. A ring oscillator uses an odd number of inverting delay stages; each stage adds delay, and the loop oscillates when the total phase is 180° plus inversion. Ring VCOs are small in CMOS but have low Q, so their phase noise is worse. To analyse a feedback oscillator: break the loop, calculate Aβ(jω), find the frequency where phase is 0°, check |Aβ| ≥ 1 there, then confirm the steady-state amplitude by saturation or a limiting circuit.

sections.h3: VCO tuning, KVCO and phase noise

blocks.text: A voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) changes frequency with a tuning voltage: f_out = f_0 + K_VCO V_tune. f_0 is the centre frequency in Hz, K_VCO is the tuning sensitivity in Hz/V, and V_tune is the control voltage. The tuning range is f_min to f_max. K_VCO is not perfectly constant because a varactor is nonlinear; see 5.1. A large K_VCO gives wide tuning but also turns small control noise into frequency modulation.

Phase noise is the single-sideband noise power in a 1 Hz bandwidth at offset Δf from the carrier, divided by the carrier power. It is written L(Δf) and measured in dBc/Hz: dB relative to the carrier, per hertz. The Leeson model gives the shape.

blocks.where: F is the device noise factor; k is Boltzmann's constant (1.38×10⁻²³ J/K); T is absolute temperature in K; P_s is the oscillator signal power in W; Q is the loaded tank quality factor; f_c is the flicker corner frequency; Δf is the offset from the carrier in Hz.

blocks.text: Far from the carrier the term in f_0²/Δf² gives a 1/f² slope: 20 dB per decade. Close in, flicker adds a 1/f³ slope: 30 dB per decade. Higher Q and higher P_s lower the noise. The figure plots example densities at 1 kHz to 1 MHz offsets.

A phase-locked loop (PLL) makes a stable, tuneable output from a clean reference. A phase-frequency detector (PFD) compares the reference frequency f_ref with the divided VCO frequency f_vco/N. A charge pump converts the phase error into current pulses. The loop filter turns that current into the VCO control voltage and sets the loop bandwidth. The divider sets N.

In lock, the feedback forces f_vco/N = f_ref, so f_out = N f_ref. An integer-N synthesizer uses a whole-number N; its channel spacing equals f_ref. A fractional-N synthesizer uses N = N_int + K/M, where K/M is a fraction set by a modulus; this gives finer spacing without a very low reference. Only a few universities teach fractional-N detail; the cost is fractional spurs, which need a DAC or dithering to reduce.

The loop bandwidth f_L decides which source dominates. Inside f_L, the PLL copies the reference noise multiplied by N and suppresses VCO noise. Outside f_L, the output follows the free-running VCO. A wide loop gives fast lock but passes more reference noise; a narrow loop gives clean close-in output but slow lock. Lock time is roughly a few cycles of 1/f_L. Spurs appear at f_ref, at fractional frequencies, and at multiples.

figure.caption: Phase noise density against offset for the free-running VCO and the reference oscillator before multiplication. At 1 MHz offset the reference is −150 dBc/Hz; after adding 46 dB for N = 200 it becomes −104 dBc/Hz, close to the VCO's −100 dBc/Hz.

spec.aria: Phase noise versus offset frequency for a free-running VCO and the reference oscillator before multiplication, using the example offset values.

examples.question: A 2 GHz VCO has phase noise −100 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset. A PLL uses a 10 MHz reference and N = 200. The reference phase noise is −150 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset. (a) Estimate the multiplied reference phase noise at 1 MHz offset. (b) Compare it with the free-running VCO. (c) If the PLL loop bandwidth is 100 kHz, which source sets the output phase noise at 1 MHz?
steps: 1. Find N: N = f_vco / f_ref = 2×10⁹ Hz / 10×10⁶ Hz = 200.
2. Frequency multiplication by N raises phase noise by 20 log₁₀ N = 20 log₁₀ 200 = 46.02 dB.
3. Multiplied reference phase noise = −150 + 46.02 = −103.98 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset.
4. Compare: VCO is −100 dBc/Hz. Difference = −100 − (−103.98) = 3.98 dB; the reference path is 3.98 dB lower (better).
5. Loop bandwidth = 100 kHz. The 1 MHz offset is ten times outside the loop, so the PLL output there is set mainly by the VCO, not by the reference path.
examples.answer: The multiplied reference is about −103.98 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset, 3.98 dB below the free-running VCO; with a 100 kHz loop bandwidth the VCO dominates at 1 MHz because that offset is outside the loop.
examples.check:
import math
N = 200
add = 20 * math.log10(N)
mult = -150 + add
diff = -100 - mult
print(N)
print(round(add, 2))
print(round(mult, 2))
print(round(diff, 2))

traps: dBc/Hz is a density at one offset, not total integrated phase noise. Integrating over the loop bandwidth is a separate step.
Multiplication adds 20 log₁₀N to phase noise, not 10 log₁₀N. The 20 comes from voltage; 10 would be a power ratio without squaring.
A PLL does not remove reference noise. Inside the loop bandwidth the reference noise appears multiplied by N; outside, the VCO dominates.
K_VCO is in Hz/V or MHz/V; control voltage noise in V becomes frequency deviation in Hz. Keep units consistent.
Integer-N channel spacing is f_ref; fractional-N can have finer spacing but produces fractional spurs. Do not call all PLLs integer-N.

quiz.q: State the Barkhausen condition for oscillation.
quiz.a: The loop gain magnitude must be at least one and the loop phase shift must be 0° or a whole number of 360°: |Aβ| ≥ 1 at ∠0°.

quiz.q: Why does a higher loaded Q reduce phase noise at a fixed offset?
quiz.a: A higher Q makes the tank more selective. The Leeson term 1 + f_0²/(4Q²Δf²) is smaller, so noise at offset Δf is lower. The 1/f² corner moves closer to the carrier.

quiz.q: A 100 MHz reference has phase noise −140 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz offset. It is multiplied to 2 GHz. Find N and the multiplied phase noise at 100 kHz offset.
quiz.a: N = 2 GHz / 100 MHz = 20. Addition = 20 log₁₀ 20 = 26.02 dB. Multiplied phase noise = −140 + 26.02 = −113.98 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz offset.

quiz.q: A PLL has loop bandwidth 50 kHz. The multiplied reference noise is −110 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz and −120 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz; the free VCO is −90 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz and −115 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz. Which source sets output phase noise at each offset?
quiz.a: At 10 kHz, inside the 50 kHz loop, the reference path sets the output; the VCO is suppressed. At 1 MHz, outside the loop, the VCO sets the output; the reference path is attenuated.
It is noise power in a 1 Hz bandwidth at a given offset from the carrier, expressed in dB relative to the carrier power.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of fractional-N over integer-N.
quiz.a: Advantage: finer channel spacing without a very low reference frequency. Disadvantage: fractional spurs and more complex calibration or dithering.

quiz.q: A VCO has K_VCO = 50 MHz/V. The tune voltage changes by 0.4 V. Find the frequency change.
quiz.a: Δf = K_VCO × ΔV = 50 MHz/V × 0.4 V = 20 MHz.

quiz.q: Why does widening PLL loop bandwidth reduce lock time but increase reference-noise contribution?
quiz.a: Lock time is roughly a few cycles of 1/f_L, so a wider loop locks faster. A wider loop also copies the multiplied reference noise over a wider band, so more reference noise reaches the output.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, phase-noise budgets are built in PLL design tools and checked on a phase-noise analyzer. 5G and Wi-Fi radios use fractional-N synthesizers with digital calibration; radar uses low-noise VCOs for FMCW chirps. Search terms: Leeson model, integer boundary spur, charge-pump PLL, VCO tuning range, phase-noise analyzer.
